To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the incorporation of amino acid precursors from the neuronal and glial pools was increased and decreased, respectively, following electrical stimulation in the brain.

the stimulation of peripheral nerves causes a large increase in the incorporation of glucose‐derived amino acids into proteins of synaptosomal membranes and a decrease in the incorporation of acetate‐derived amino acids in vivo and in vitro.
the electrical stimulation of the peripheral nerve increases the incorporation of carbon into proteins in the sensorimotor cortex in vivo, using the neuronal precursor [14C] glucose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a specific effect of electrical stimuli on protein synthesis in the brain.
the effect of BPS on the incorporation of amino acid precursors from both neuronal and glia cell compartments into brain proteins in vivo and in vitro.
the effect of electrical stimulation of afferents to the brain on the incorporation of amino acid precursors into brain proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

BPS results in a significant increase in the incorporation of 14C into brain proteins when [14C] glucose is the precursor, and in a significant decrease of the incorporation of 1C from [14C]-acetate, [4‐3 H]phenylalanine or [U‐14 C]leucine.

the incorporation of carbon into brain proteins is stimulated by afferent electrical stimulation of the cortex, using [14C] glucose as the precursor, whereas the incorporation of carbon is depressed using [14Cacetate as the precursor.

the incorporation of amino acid precursors from the neuronal and glial cell compartments into the proteins of the brain is differentially affected by BPS, with an increase of incorporation from neuronal and a decrease from glial precursors, and that the changes are mediated through the activation of the peripheral nerve terminals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the incorporation of carbon into brain proteins following BPS is dependent on the nature of the precursor injected and on the route of its administration, with a significant increase in incorporation of carbon from glucose and a significant decrease from acetate in vivo.
electrical stimuli in the brain result in increased protein synthesis in the contralaterally stimulated area, but not in the ipsilaterally stimulated cortex.
BPS causes a large increase in the incorporation of glucose‐derived amino acids into brain protein in vivo and in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the incorporation of amino acid precursors into brain proteins is differentially affected by electrical stimulation depending on the nature of the precursor and the site of incorporation.

the stimulation of peripheral nerves in the anaesthetised animal results in a large increase in the incorporation of glucose‐derived carbon into proteins in the contraversive hemisphere, but a decrease in the incorporation of acetate‐derived carbon.

the stimulation of a peripheral nerve causes a significant increase in the incorporation of 14C into proteins in the sensorimotor cortex using both neuronal and glia specific amino acid precursors in vivo and in vitro.
